1.pericope_label: And when the seventh month was come, and the children of Israel were in the cities, the people gathered themselves together as one man to Jerusalem. Then stood up Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren the priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and his brethren, and builded the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings thereon, as it is written in the law of Moses the man of God. And they set the altar upon his bases; for fear was upon them because of the people of those countries: and they offered burnt offerings thereon unto the Lord, even burnt offerings morning and evening. They kept also the feast of tabernacles, as it is written, and offered the daily burnt offerings by number, according to the custom, as the duty of every day required; And afterward offered the continual burnt offering, both of the new moons, and of all the set feasts of the Lord that were consecrated, and of every one that willingly offered a freewill offering unto the Lord. From the first day of the seventh month began they to offer burnt offerings unto the Lord. But the foundation of the temple of the Lord was not yet laid. They gave money also unto the masons, and to the carpenters; and meat, and drink, and oil, unto them of Zidon, and to them of Tyre, to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea of Joppa, according to the grant that they had of Cyrus king of Persia.

schools.summary: Ellicott begins with the rendering, that the seventh month approached rather than was come, and sets the season: Tisri, answering to our September, was the most solemn month of the year, holding both the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles, the latter afterwards distinguished as the feast pre-eminently; as one man he glosses not as all of them but as with one consent. The altar he treats as only the beginning of the work, the temple being as it were built around it as the centre of all, and its setting as the discovery of the old site among the ruins, by which all the new was signified to be a restoration of the old. The fear he reads forward rather than back: until their offerings went up they did not feel sure of the divine protection, this was their first act of defiance in the presence of the nations around, and near the altar they were strong. He takes the summary of new moons and set feasts as general and anticipatory, the essentials of ritual being fixed, like the arrangements in Leviticus, before the temple was built, and he presses the notes of time, the altar raised before the month came and the daily sacrifice offered from the first day until the Feast of Tabernacles began. On the payments he observes that their own workmen were paid in money while the Phoenicians, as in Solomon's days, were paid in kind, and that Joppa was the port to which the cedar came by sea and thence thirty-five miles inland. Delitzsch supplies the chronology the text omits: the year is not stated but the year of the return from Babylon is intended, as appears from the dating of the foundation; the clause about the children of Israel being in the cities is circumstantial; and since the burnt offerings began on the first day of the month, the altar must have been completed by that day, which agrees with the month having only approached. On the setting he rules against the English, holding that the Hebrew says upon its former place and not upon its bases, the marginal plural being an incorrect revision, and he explains the construction behind the fear as a being in a condition, a being in fear having lain upon them. The purpose he states plainly: they erected the altar and restored the worship of Jahve in order to secure the divine protection, because fear of the surrounding heathen population had fallen upon them. The burnt offering day by day according to number he identifies with the offerings commanded for the several days of the festival, and the freewill offering as one brought from inclination, which might be presented any day but chiefly followed the prescribed sacrifices at the annual feasts. The grant of Cyrus he limits to the permission to rebuild, since nothing is said of any special grant with respect to timber.

Gill reads the opening with the same grammatical care as the critics and reaches their conclusion: the month Tisri answers to part of September and October, or rather the month was approaching, for before it was actually come the people had met and an altar had been built, since on the first day of it sacrifices were offered. Jeshua he identifies as the high priest and the proper person to give the lead in the work. On the bases he allows either sense, that they might remain of the old altar, or that the meaning is simply that the altar was fixed and settled on the same spot where it stood before. He is exact about the order of the sacrifices against a natural misreading: the continual burnt offering was not begun after the Feast of Tabernacles, for that they offered as soon as the altar was set up and on the first day of the month; rather, after the daily burnt offering of the morning they offered the sacrifices peculiar to the several days of the feast, never neglecting the daily offering and always beginning with it, all the rest coming after it, and so on other festivals. He fills out the calendar too, noting that the first day was not only a new moon but a grand festival, the feast of blowing of trumpets, and that no doubt they observed the tenth day with all its rites, which was the Day of Atonement, and that the feast of tabernacles began on the fifteenth day. The money given to the masons and carpenters he explains as money to buy stone and timber with for the building of the temple.

Clarke reconstructs the months the narrative passes over. The Israelites seem to have left Babylon about the spring of the year; on arrival at Jerusalem they constructed themselves huts and sheds to lodge in among the ruins, in which they must have spent some months; after this they rebuilt the altar of burnt offerings, kept the Feast of Tabernacles, which happened about that time, and continued to offer sacrifices regularly as if the temple were standing. He fixes Tisri as answering to the latter part of our September and the beginning of October, identifies Jeshua as the grandson of Seraiah the high priest whom Nebuchadnezzar put to death and as the first high priest after the captivity, and explains the priority of the altar by necessity: worship had to be kept up during the whole time they should be employed in re-edifying the temple, and all this they did though fear was upon them because of the unfriendly disposition of their surrounding neighbours. The altar he places on the same spot on which it had formerly stood, the regular offerings from the first day of the month with the feast following on the fifteenth, and the offerings religiously continued all the time they were building. The payments he reads as deliberate imitation, that they copied the conduct of Solomon, employing the Tyrians and giving them meat and drink, which they now had permission from Cyrus to do. Wesley calls it a sacred kind of month wherein there were divers festivals for which the people had been preparing themselves, and makes the altar of more present necessity than the temple on three grounds, to make atonement to God for all their sins, to obtain God's assistance for the building of the temple, and to strengthen their own hearts and hands in that great work. The fear he takes as a spur: so they made the more haste lest they should be hindered, and apprehension of dangers should quicken us in our duty, for if we have many enemies we have the more need to have God for our friend and to keep up our correspondence with him. The feast he supposes named for all the solemnities of the month, since it is not probable they would neglect the Day of Atonement, so severely enjoined and so exceedingly suitable to their present condition. On the offerings he measures zeal by poverty: the law required much, but they offered more, for though they had little wealth they had much zeal, and happy are they that bring with them out of the furnace of affliction such a holy heat as this.

Henry reads the assembly as voluntary and the zeal as the point. They probably came from Babylon in the spring, and at least four months must be allowed for the journey, so the seventh month soon came; and then they gathered themselves together by agreement among themselves rather than by the command of authority. Though they had newly come to their cities and had their hands full of providing necessaries for themselves and their families, which might have excused them from attending on God's altar till the hurry was over, as many foolishly put off their coming to the communion till they are settled in the world, such was their zeal, now that they had newly come from under correction for their irreligion, that they left all their business in the country to attend God's altar; and in this pious zeal they were all of a mind, they came as one man. Let worldly business be postponed to the business of religion, he adds, and it will prosper the better. From the altar built in the same place, upon the same bases, he draws two lessons: to begin with God, since the more difficult and necessitous our case the more concerned we are to take him along with us in all our ways, and if we expect to be directed by his oracles let him be honoured by our offerings; and to do what we can in the worship of God when we cannot do what we would, for they could not immediately have a temple but would not be without an altar, as Abraham built one wherever he came. On the fear he offers both readings and commends each: though they were in the midst of enemies that bore ill will to them and their religion, yet they built the altar and would not be frightened from their religion by the opposition they were likely to meet with, and never let the fear of man bring us into this snare; and because they were in such danger therefore they set it up, since apprehension of danger should stir us up to our duty, and this good use we should make of our fears, that we should be driven by them to our knees. He notes that the altar was reared to be used and used accordingly, that those who have an altar should not starve it, that it does not appear they had any fire from heaven as Moses and Solomon had but that common fire served them as it did the patriarchs, and that having begun they kept up the continual burnt offering morning and evening, having known by sad experience what it was to want the comfort of the daily sacrifice to plead in their daily prayers, the daily lamb typifying the Lamb of God whose righteousness must be our confidence in all our prayers. The Feast of Tabernacles he finds doubly seasonable, now that they had received such great mercy, and now that they were beginning to settle in their cities, since it might serve to remind them of their fathers dwelling in tents in the wilderness.

debates: Whether the seventh month had come or was only drawing near, where Ellicott renders the opening as approached and Gill and Delitzsch argue the same from the narrative itself, since the people had met and the altar had been finished before the first day on which the offerings began, while Clarke and Henry take the month as simply come and place the gathering inside it.

What it means that they set the altar upon his bases, where Gill allows either the bases remaining of the old altar or simply the old spot, Clarke and Ellicott take it for the former site, which Ellicott supposes was discovered among the ruins so that all the new was signified to be a restoration of the old, and Delitzsch rules the English rendering out, holding that the Hebrew says upon its former place and that the marginal plural is an incorrect revision.

What follows from the fear that was upon them, where Wesley and Clarke make it a spur to haste and a circumstance braved, Ellicott and Delitzsch make the altar the means of securing the divine protection and read the act as their first open defiance before the surrounding nations, and Henry offers both readings together, that they built although they were afraid and that they built because they were afraid.
outliers: Ellicott observes that their own workmen were paid in money while the Phoenicians, as in Solomon's days, were paid in kind.
Henry notes that it does not appear they had any fire from heaven, as Moses and Solomon had, but that common fire served them as it did the patriarchs.

8.pericope_label: Now in the second year of their coming unto the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, began Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and the remnant of their brethren the priests and the Levites, and all they that were come out of the captivity unto Jerusalem; and appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to set forward the work of the house of the Lord. Then stood Jeshua with his sons and his brethren, Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together, to set forward the workmen in the house of God: the sons of Henadad, with their sons and their brethren the Levites. And when the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the Lord, they set the priests in their apparel with trumpets, and the Levites the sons of Asaph with cymbals, to praise the Lord, after the ordinance of David king of Israel. And they sang together by course in praising and giving thanks unto the Lord; because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel. And all the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the Lord, because the foundation of the house of the Lord was laid. But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy: So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people: for the people shouted with a loud shout, and the noise was heard afar off.

schools.summary: Delitzsch dates the beginning from the return rather than the reign: in the second year of their coming to the house of God at Jerusalem, that is, after their arrival from Babylon, Zerubbabel and Joshua began by appointing the Levites from twenty years old and upwards to the oversight of the building, which is to say that the work was taken in hand; whether that second year of the return coincides with the second year of Cyrus he declines to decide. On the names he is at his most technical. He counts three classes of Levites, Jeshua with his sons and brethren, Kadmiel with his sons, and the sons of Henadad with their sons and brethren; he observes that the singular verb stands before a plural subject, as often when the verb precedes; and from the comparison with the earlier register he concludes that the sons of Judah is a clerical error for the sons of Hodaviah, which is a more precise designation of the sons of Kadmiel only and not, as Bertheau would have it, a comprehensive appellation for all hitherto enumerated. He renders the word for together as one, that is, all without exception, and notes that the sons of Henadad are not expressly named among those who returned. The ceremony he describes from the construction of the verbs: when the builders laid the foundation, then Zerubbabel and Joshua, the heads of the community, set the priests clothed in their robes of office with trumpets and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the Lord after the ordinance of David. On the ages he does the arithmetic, Solomon's temple having been destroyed about half a century before the foundation of this one was laid, so that the older men present might possibly have seen the former house. The last verse he guards against a natural misreading: the meaning is not that the people could not hear the weeping of the older priests and Levites and heads of the people because it was overpowered by the rejoicing of the multitude, but that among the people also a shout of joy and a voice of weeping arose together, and that the rejoicing was so loud the two could not be distinguished from each other. Ellicott dates it from the reign instead, the second year of Cyrus being their second year in the holy place, and finds the month significant, Zif being chosen apparently because it was the same month in which Solomon laid the first foundation, while the appointment of the Levites to superintend and the age fixed for it are in strict harmony with the original ordinances of David. He leaves the disputed reading standing, taking Jeshua and Kadmiel, both of the stock of Judah or Hodaviah, as the two heads of Levitical families whose fewness is compensated by their unanimity and vigour, and he reports that Henadad is absent from the earlier list though a Levitical name elsewhere, and that why it is omitted there or inserted here cannot be determined. The music he refers wholly to precedent, since all goes back to earlier times: as the first offerings on the altar were according to what was written in the law of Moses, so the musical ceremonial of this foundation follows the precedent of David, the trumpets belonging to the priests and the cymbals to the Levites in the ancient ordinances of worship. The singing by course he explains as answering each other in chorus, or antiphonally, and the shouting as religious acclamation. On the weeping he is restrained: the scene requires the comment of the later prophets, and the grief of the ancients was not occasioned by any comparison as to size and grandeur, unless indeed they marked the smallness of their foundation stones, for they thought chiefly of the great desolation as measured by the past, while the younger people thought of the new future.

Gill accounts for the whole interval between the two months. The Jews seem to have set out from Babylon in the spring of the preceding year, as it was now of this; the journey to Jerusalem was about four months, as Ezra performed it, though it might take longer for such a body of people, being larger than the company that came with him; wherefore after they had visited their respective cities and settled their affairs there they came to Jerusalem in the seventh month and kept the Feast of Tabernacles, and then returned to their cities again, the winter season being an improper time to begin the building of the temple, having given money to workmen to purchase materials and no doubt left a sufficient number to clear away the rubbish and get things ready by the returning spring to set about the work. On the names he gives the warning briefly, that this is not Jeshua the high priest before mentioned but Jeshua the Levite, and he identifies the builders who laid the foundation as the masons, whose work it was. The singing by course he explains as singing by turns in responses and answering one another, as the word signifies, so that when one company had performed their part another took theirs. The ancient men he reckons at seventy or eighty years of age. On the last verse he reads the confusion as acoustic: the people could not discern the one noise from the other clearly and distinctly, they were so mixed and confounded together, and made such a jarring and discord.

Clarke accounts for the interval as the time of preparation, which had been employed in clearing the ground, felling timber, hewing stones and transporting them to the place, and making other necessary preparations for the commencement of the building. The music he refers to David's own composition, that the praise was offered with psalms which he composed, acting in the manner which he directed. On the weeping he is the fullest of the commentators and the most unsparing: they saw that the glory had departed from Israel; in their circumstances it was impossible to build such a house as the first temple was; and had this been even possible, it would still have been greatly inferior, because it wanted the ark of the covenant, the heavenly fire, the mercy seat, the heavenly manna, Aaron's rod that budded, the divine presence, the spirit of prophecy, and most probably the Urim and Thummim. The shouting he explains by age and experience, that those who shouted found themselves now restored to their own land and to the worship of their God in his own peculiar city, and that these in general had not seen the original temple and therefore could not feel affected in the way the elderly people did. The sight he judges must have been very affecting, a whole people, one part crying aloud with sorrow, the other shouting aloud for joy, and on the same occasion too, in which both sides felt an equal interest; and he points forward to the prophet who comforted them by assuring them that the glory of this latter house should exceed that of the former. Wesley gives the same warning about the name, that this Joshua is not the high priest so called but a Levite, and glosses the commission to set forward as encouraging them to a vigorous prosecution of the work. The hymn he calls that everlasting hymn which will never be out of date and to which our tongue should never be out of tune, adding that whatever our condition is let it be owned that God is good, and whatever fails, that his mercy fails not. The weeping he itemises in four counts: the poor preparations made for this house in comparison of what was made for the other; the want of those things which were the principal glory of the former temple, namely the ark and the Urim and Thummim; foundation stones far inferior to the former both for quantity and price; and foundations of a far narrower compass, since although the foundations of the house strictly so called were of equal largeness with those of the former, the foundations of the whole building belonging to the first temple were far larger than these. The mixture of sorrow and joy he takes for a representation of this world: in heaven all are singing and none sighing, in hell all are wailing and none rejoicing, but here on earth we can scarce discern the shouts of joy from the noise of the weeping, so let us learn to rejoice with them that rejoice and weep with them that weep, and meantime let us ourselves rejoice as though we rejoiced not and weep as though we wept not.

Henry notes first that there was no dispute among the returned Jews whether they should build the temple, for that was immediately resolved on and that it should be done with all speed, since what comfort could they take in their own land if they had not that token of God's presence with them and the record of his name among them. The timing he presses as zeal: they began as soon as ever the season of the year would permit and when they had ended the solemnities of the passover, taking little more than half a year for the preparation of ground and materials, so much were their hearts upon it; and when any good work is to be done it will be our wisdom to set about it quickly and not to lose time, yea though we foresee difficulty and opposition in it, for thus we engage ourselves to it and engage God for us, and well begun is half ended. On the agents he observes that the work of God is likely to go on well when magistrates, ministers and people are hearty for it and agree in their places to promote it, and that it was God who gave them one heart for this service; and of the Levites appointed to set forward the work by setting forward the workmen and strengthening their hands with good and comfortable words, that those who do not work themselves may yet do good service by quickening and encouraging those who do. The music he reads as instrumental to the words, the priests with the trumpets appointed by Moses and the Levites with the cymbals appointed by David making up a concert not to please the ear but to assist the singing of that everlasting hymn which will never be out of date and to which our tongues should never be out of tune, that God is good and his mercy endures for ever: let all the streams of mercy be traced up to the fountain, and whatever our condition is, how many soever our griefs and fears, let it be owned that God is good, and whatever fails, that his mercy fails not; and let the reviving of the church's interests, when they seemed dead, be ascribed to the continuance of that mercy for ever, for therefore the church continues. The two cries he treats as different sentiments among the people of God, each expressing himself according to his sentiments, and yet with no disagreement among them, their minds not alienated from each other nor the common concern retarded by it. Those who only knew the misery of having no temple at all praised the Lord with shouts of joy when they saw but the foundation of one laid, to whom even this seemed great and was as life from the dead, and to their hungry souls even this was sweet; and we ought to be thankful for the beginnings of mercy though we have not yet come to the perfection of it. Those who remembered the glory of the first temple lamented the disproportion, and there was some reason for it, so that if they turned their tears into the right channel and bewailed the sin that was the cause of this melancholy change they did well, since sin sullies the glory of any church or people; yet it was their infirmity to mingle those tears with the common joys and so to cast a damp upon them, for they despised the day of small things and were unthankful for the good they enjoyed because it was not so much as their ancestors had, though it was much more than they deserved, and in the harmony of public joys let not us be jarring strings.

debates: What the disputed designation of the Levites is, where Delitzsch concludes from the earlier register that the sons of Judah is a clerical error for the sons of Hodaviah and applies it to the sons of Kadmiel alone, against Bertheau's reading of it as a comprehensive appellation for all hitherto enumerated, while Ellicott leaves the reading standing and takes Jeshua and Kadmiel both as of the stock of Judah, or Hodaviah, two heads of Levitical families whose fewness is compensated by their unanimity and vigour.

Why the old men wept, where Wesley itemises the poor preparations, the want of the ark and the Urim and Thummim, foundation stones inferior in quantity and price, and foundations of a narrower compass, and Clarke says the glory had departed since even a grander house would still have wanted the ark, the heavenly fire, the mercy seat and the spirit of prophecy, while Ellicott nearly denies the comparison, allowing only that they may have marked the smallness of their foundation stones and locating the grief in the great desolation as measured by the past, and Henry grants the tears some reason in the sin that caused the change but calls their indulgence an infirmity that cast a damp on the common joy.

What the last verse reports, where Delitzsch insists it does not mean the weeping was drowned by the rejoicing but that among the people too both cries were raised at once, Gill reads the two noises as so mixed and confounded as to make a jarring discord, and Wesley with Henry takes the mixture for a representation of this world, where we can scarce discern the shouts of joy from the noise of the weeping.
outliers: Ellicott finds the month itself significant, Zif being apparently chosen because it was the same month in which Solomon laid the first foundation.
Clarke refers the praise to psalms David had himself composed, the singers acting in the manner which he directed.
